trendStories.title: 改变我世界的十行代码
trendStories.originalTitle: Ten Lines Of Code That Changed My World
trendStories.fullContent:
Ten lines of code that, one way or another, mean something to me. Either because I wrote them, or I extensively copied them, or they made me laugh. Or cry.

I don’t know when I typed this for the first time, or if it was exactly this version. Might have been without the comma, or with more exclamation marks.

Nevertheless, the computer obliged, cheerfully greeting the world, and very much in particular, the wide-eyed kid who had just communicated with a computer for the first time.

The second line drove home the point that a computer will do anything you tell it to. Hello world forever!

Copy the line and paste it your browser’s console for a crossover between old school pop culture TV and nerdy coding humor, with a big fat dose of “JavaScript is stupid” on top.

A classic, and a genuine LOL when I first ran it.

Machine language is as close to the metal as it gets. No warnings, no logs, no guardrails. It even allows you to modify itself, by overwriting the actual bytes of the code while it runs.

Like in this example, where you update the high bytes of the source and destination addresses. The branch loops from $2000 to $20FF, and the subsequent INC changes the address from $2000 to $2100, before starting the loop again.

(The 6502 is little endian, so we do +2 and +5 instead of +1 and +4)

As low-level as it gets, hardcore, and slightly dangerous. Realizing you could do this really drove home the point that, when coding this close to the metal, anything goes.

This tiny batch script allowed for a poor man’s touch on Windows, which I used extensively from Windows NT to Windows 7. I typed touch filename.txt in the Total Commander mini-shell to quickly generate new, empty files. Couldn’t live without it.

The console.log of the cascades! The var_dump() of the styles! The printf() of the sheets!

Just poke a specific byte into the right place of the binary code currently in the computer’s memory, and you suddenly get infinite lives, enegry or money.

Not only did this allow you to cheat at the game, it also brought the powerful realization that everything in any game could be manipulated, as long as you knew where to PEEK and POKE.

A funny story, and for those of us who ever had to toil away on boring, aimless projects, an idea that might have its appeal.

If you ran into a problem with Linux around the 2000s, you often took to IRC in search for help. It was there that many found the magic cure to all Linux problems, which was always the same: log in as root, and run rm -rf /.

Without fail, it made every Linux problem dissappear!

It was the early 90s and our school finally set up a LAN, so of course my cyberpunk scriptkiddies lamers 1337 h4x0rz buddies and I explored it. We knew that all usernames consisted of three letters, and those not in use would be left at the default password.

So we whipped up this extremely crude username scanner in Borland Pascal. More bugs than lines of code, but it sorta did the job. (And it should — it’s version 2.00 after all!)

We happily hacked all the dormant accounts we could find, and then… moved on.

An animated poem in nothing but 280 characters of CSS. No JavaScript, not even HTML — it would run in an empty document with just a <style> block, and these 280 characters of pure CSS.

The artifical limit was a step up from the earlier 140 character limit, dictated by Twitter, allowing small snippets of code to be posted that you could copy over to an empty CodePen to see an amusing effect.

I’m especially proud of the 1e+9 duration, which is shorter than infinite (both in time as in character count).
trendStories.fullTranslation:
十行以某种方式对我而言意义非凡的代码。要么是因为我亲自写下了它们，要么是我曾大量抄录过它们，又或者是它们曾让我开怀大笑，亦或泪流满面。

我不记得自己第一次敲出这段代码是什么时候了，也不确定是否就是这个精确的版本。当时可能没有逗号，或者有更多的感叹号。

尽管如此，计算机还是照做了，欢快地向世界打了个招呼，尤其是向那个第一次与计算机产生交流、睁大双眼的孩子问好。

第二行代码让人深刻体会到：只要你发出指令，计算机就会照单全收。永远的 Hello World！

把这行代码复制并粘贴到你浏览器的控制台中，你将见证老派流行文化电视与极客编程幽默的跨界碰撞，外加一剂浓烈醇厚的“JavaScript 真是太蠢了”的调侃。

经典之作，我第一次运行它时真的是笑出了声。

机器语言是能达到的最接近硬件底层的语言。没有警告，没有日志，也没有任何防护栏。它甚至允许你自我修改——在代码运行时直接覆写其底层的实际字节。

就像这个例子一样，你在其中更新了源地址和目的地址的高位字节。分支语句从 $2000 循环到 $20FF，随后的 INC 在重新开始循环之前，将地址从 $2000 修改为 $2100。

（6502 处理器采用小端序，因此我们使用的是 +2 和 +5，而不是 +1 和 +4）

底层的极致，硬核，且略带危险性。意识到自己可以做到这一点，让人切实体会到：当你在如此接近硬件底层的地方编程时，一切皆有可能。

这个微型批处理脚本在 Windows 上实现了简易版的 touch 功能，从 Windows NT 到 Windows 7 期间我一直在高频使用它。我在 Total Commander 的微型 shell 中输入 touch filename.txt，就能快速生成新的空白文件。简直须臾不可或缺。

层叠样式界的 console.log！样式表里的 var_dump()！CSS 领域的 printf()！

只要把一个特定的字节写入当前计算机内存中二进制代码的恰当位置，你就能瞬间获得无限生命、无限能量或无限金钱。

这不仅能让你在游戏中作弊，还带来了一种震撼的认知：只要你知道在哪里 PEEK 和 POKE，任何游戏中的一切都可以被肆意操控。

一个有趣的故事，而对于我们这些曾经不得不埋头于无聊、漫无目的的项目的人来说，这或许是一个颇具吸引力的点子。

在 2000 年代前后，如果你在 Linux 上遇到问题，往往会去 IRC 寻求帮助。正是在那里，许多人找到了解决所有 Linux 问题的神奇妙方，而且答案始终如一：以 root 身份登录，然后运行 rm -rf /。

百试百灵，它能让每一个 Linux 问题都彻底消失！

那是在 90 年代初，我们的学校终于搭建了局域网，因此我那帮赛博朋克、脚本小子、菜鸟、骨灰级黑客伙伴们和我自然对其进行了一番探索。我们知道所有的用户名都由三个字母组成，而那些未启用的账户则会保留默认密码。

于是我们在 Borland Pascal 中捣鼓出了这个极其简陋的用户名扫描器。Bug 比代码行数还多，但它大致还能用。（按理也该如此——毕竟这可是 2.00 版本！）

我们开开心心地黑掉了能找到的所有休眠账户，然后……就去干别的事了。

一首仅用 280 个字符的 CSS 编写的动画诗篇。没有 JavaScript，甚至没有 HTML——它可以在一个仅包含一个块级元素的空白文档中运行，全凭这 280 个纯粹的 CSS 字符。

这个人为限制是由 Twitter 设定的，相比早期的 140 字符限制有所放宽，它允许用户发布简短的代码片段，你可以将其复制到一个空白的 CodePen 中来欣赏有趣的视觉效果。

我尤其对自己使用的 1e+9 持续时间感到自豪，它比 infinite（无限）还要短（无论是在时间意义上，还是在字符数量上）。

trendStories.fullContent:
With its garish ‘grellow’ colour, mythological origins, secret recipe and limited supplies, the herbal liqueur made by French monks is now the coolest thing to order at the bar

It’s just after 9pm in drizzly Belleville, Paris. Too late for cocktails, too early for bedtime, but up the steep hill that straddles the 19th and 20th arrondissements, digestif hour is in sight.

In the past few years, more and more Parisians have been reaching for a glass of Chartreuse, an intensely green/yellow herbal liqueur with a folkloric backstory involving Carthusian monks, cholera and a recipe of omertà-like secrecy.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
凭借其耀眼的“黄绿色调”、神话般的起源、绝密配方以及有限的供应量，这款由法国修道士酿造的草本利口酒，如今已成为酒吧里点单最酷的选择。

细雨蒙蒙的巴黎贝尔维尔（Belleville），时间刚过晚上9点。喝鸡尾酒嫌晚，上床睡觉又嫌早，但在横跨第19区和第20区的陡峭山坡上，餐后消化酒的时刻即将到来。

过去几年里，越来越多的巴黎人开始端起一杯查特酒（Chartreuse）——这是一种浓郁的黄绿色草本利口酒，流传着与加尔都西会修道士、霍乱以及恪守如黑帮“缄默法则”（omertà）般严格保密配方相关的民间传奇故事。

trendStories.fullContent:
It might seem like self-preservation, but the results aren’t necessarily what you’d expect

In Dr Seuss’s Green Eggs and Ham , the relentlessly upbeat Sam-I-Am spends the entire book badgering a grouchy, nameless narrator into tasting the eponymous dish. He cycles through one inventive but futile pitch after another – in a house, with a mouse, in a box, with a fox, on a train, in the rain – until the narrator, caving just to get some peace, tastes the dish and discovers he loves it. When my son was growing up, “Green Eggs and Ham” was my shorthand for telling him he was avoiding something he’d love if he only tried it.

Of course, not every experience we fear or dread turns out to be a delicious surprise. Misery is an inescapable part of the human condition. We can’t avoid it, yet people try their hardest anyway. We cling to hope even when a situation is hopeless. We push painful thoughts out of mind rather than confront them. We struggle to control things that cannot be changed. And we go to sometimes self-destructive lengths to protect our pride from even the tiniest pinprick. These strategies may sometimes spare us pain in the moment. But while they are intended to promote (or at least preserve) our happiness, over time they have the perverse result of making us much more miserable.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
这看似是一种自我保护，但结果未必如你所料。

在苏斯博士的《绿鸡蛋和火腿》（Green Eggs and Ham）中，永远乐观的“我是山姆”（Sam-I-Am）整本书都在纠缠一个脾气暴躁、没有名字的讲述者，劝他尝尝这道与书名同名的菜肴。他不断提出一个又一个极具创意却徒劳无功的推销——在房子里吃，和老鼠一起吃，在盒子里吃，和狐狸一起吃，在火车上吃，在雨里吃——直到这位讲述者仅仅为了耳根清净而妥协，尝了这道菜，结果发现自己爱上了它。在我儿子成长的过程中，“绿鸡蛋和火腿”成了我的代名词，用来告诉他：他正在逃避某些只要他愿意尝试就会喜欢上的东西。

当然，并非每一种让我们恐惧或畏缩的经历最终都会变成美妙的惊喜。痛苦是人类生存境况中不可避免的一部分。我们无法避开它，然而人们无论如何都会拼尽全力去逃避。即便处境毫无希望，我们依然死死抓住希望不放；我们宁愿将痛苦的念头抛诸脑后，也不愿去直面它们；我们竭力想要掌控那些根本无法改变的事情；我们甚至有时会不惜自毁前程，去保护自己的自尊心免受哪怕最轻微的刺痛。这些策略有时或许能让我们暂时免于痛苦。然而，尽管它们的初衷是为了促进（或至少维持）我们的幸福，但长此以往，它们往往会带来适得其反的结果，让我们变得更加痛苦。

trendStories.title: 通过交付更多 CSS 提升网站性能
trendStories.originalTitle: Improving site performance by shipping more CSS
trendStories.fullContent:
How we fully migrated github.com away from CSS-in-JS.

The Primer Design System powers many of the experiences you see on GitHub today. From buttons to banners to breadcrumbs, these foundational components are required to be accessible, flexible, and performant across a wide variety of scenarios.

Back in 2023, the number of components on certain pages began to explode. This led to several performance-related challenges with our existing CSS-in-JS solution:

It became clear that the Primer team needed to address the issue at the source. We needed to find an alternative that would completely avoid the client and server costs that we were seeing with our current solution. Most importantly, any alternative we pick would need to work in a way that would avoid any breakage to GitHub during the migration.

The Primer team found a solution that met all of our criteria: CSS Modules. This format would allow us to do one of our favorite things: write and use native CSS features, while still allowing some amount of the colocation and encapsulation that we had come to expect from CSS-in-JS.

With CSS Modules, styles would be authored in a CSS file alongside the JavaScript source for the component. It would also allow us to treat all class names as local by default, preventing some of the collisions and challenges that can come from global selectors. This format also removes the need for any client or server runtime behavior. Instead, styles would roll up into CSS stylesheets that were sent as part of the HTML for a page.

However, this solution was radically different from the CSS-in-JS solution we had at the time. This change would require an update to every Primer component and every component at GitHub authored using this technique. Thankfully, design systems are a perfect vehicle to deliver this kind of change at scale.

The situation for moving towards CSS Modules was clear. The Primer team would need to deliver updates to each of its components, moving them from CSS-in-JS to CSS Modules. At the same time, updates we made to these components could not break any usage in GitHub. Finally, the underlying technique we used for CSS-in-JS also had to continue working for any components in GitHub that were currently using it.

With all these constraints in place, we decided on an incremental migration strategy that would allow us to safely ship component updates without breaking the world. For each component, our plan was to:

This process created a strong feedback loop where issues were flagged early in the process as Primer continuously delivered these changes to GitHub. The use of feature flags allowed us to do this migration safely while giving us clear signals on the performance benefits of CSS Modules.

By December 2024, all components in Primer were migrated over to CSS Modules using this process. We saw performance wins across the board, in particular:

With clear performance wins from doing this work in Primer, we began to wonder if we could see similar performance wins by doing these conversions in other parts of GitHub. Similarly, how long until we could ultimately drop support for CSS-in-JS across the company?

One of the trickiest parts about removing our CSS-in-JS solution from Primer was due to the usage of the sx prop. This prop was the way to style and customize components from Primer. Teams could provide an inline object to customize everything about the component. It represented the best and worst parts of CSS-in-JS:

As a result, the first part of our journey to move away from CSS-in-JS was to reduce sx usage across GitHub. This would allow us to immediately improve performance similar to the wins we saw when migrating Primer components. It also set us up perfectly for removing CSS-in-JS entirely from the product.

It’s important to note that, while the design system itself was officially off styled-components, a large part of the GitHub codebase itself wasn’t. With sx props having been the de facto styling standard at GitHub for years, we were looking at thousands of sx props that needed migration before we could even think of getting GitHub onto the sleek new @primer/react version which didn’t rely on styled-components.

So… how did we do this immense amount of work while increasing confidence and reducing risk? The answer: not all at once.

The original CSS migration was a little bit more nuanced than we led on: in addition to migrating the components to CSS modules, feature flagging to test in production and slowly rolling them out, we also created “wrapper” components in a transitive library we called @primer/styled-react. The whole purpose of this package was to allow sx usage into the newly migrated components. This way, the instances of the GitHub UI codebase that were using this prop could continue to consume them by importing the same component through @primer/styled-react, while we realized the performance gains of importing straight from @primer/react for the cases that didn’t.

The next phase of the migration process was as follows:

Curiously enough, while we were getting ready to undertake this massive effort, styled-components maintenance mode was announced, offering further confirmation that we were taking steps in the right direction.

The work kicked off April 2025 with a peak of ~7,760 sxprops to be migrated; we wouldn’t see it realized until May 2026. Initially, one of our great in-house developers, Ian Sanders, created a VS Code plugin that would assist with per-prop migration. A similar codemod was developed internally and utilized to migrate entire files in the GitHub codebase. The work, while requiring a bit of manual oversight and careful validation, was mostly automated. A rotation of 8 engineers migrated 6,419 props over the course of 6 months, observing Server-Side Rendering time performance gains ranging from 1% up to 22% in some pages.

In a different side of GitHub, Copilot’s capabilities were increasing exponentially. AI was getting smarter, more capable; we released Copilot coding agent and Copilot code review while this work was still underway.

By the time we picked this work back up, now April of 2026, the panorama was different; we were able to get down from 895 to 0 sxprops in the span of three weeks with a team of two engineers, relentless determination, and a whole lot of Copilot coding agents.

It was a big day: we had finally completed the sx migrations that were standing between us and full styled-components removal, years in the making… we can finally clean up these dependencies and move on to different, more exciting work, right? Wrong!

GitHub supports seven different themes, all of which offer a high contrast mode variation. All of it enabled through, you guessed it, styled-components. Before we can even think of removing these dependencies, we need to decouple our theming.

Now, this isn’t as huge a deal as it sounds. Our theming variables have always been defined in CSS through our @primer/css package, and we already planned forward for non-styled Theming when we migrated @primer/react in late 2025. It’s the JavaScript usage and utilities that are enabled by styled-components that we needed to remove. Once again, we got to work.

You know the drill by now: perform the migrations, roll it out slowly, feature flag everything. Two months and a few hiccups along the way later, we were all-systems go for dependency removal; we even feature flagged that. Better safe than sorry.

GitHub has been running on 100% CSS modules as of June 2026. The safeguards we put in place enabled us to roll out significant architectural changes safely, stress test in production, catch errors, pivot and repair efficiently, ultimately allowing us to succeed in our goals and realize great performance gains along the way.

What looked at first like a CSS migration turned out to be a gradual re-platforming of how GitHub styles, themes, and ships UI at scale. By the end, we had not only removed sx, styled-components, and styled-system from dotcom, but completed it without breaking GitHub along the way. Enhancing the performance, user experience and delight of our products continues to be top of mind for all of us here at GitHub.

Josh Black is a Software Engineer based in Austin, Texas. He loves working on Design Systems, creating accessible experiences, and eating chilaquiles.

Marie is an Atlanta-based Software Engineer on GitHub Primer. If she's not pushing pixels, she's probably pushing a carry-on into an overhead bin somewhere over the Atlantic.

If you can write down how you do your work, you can automate it. Here’s what I did to support GitHub’s APAC marketing team.

trendStories.fullTranslation:
我们是如何将 github.com 完全迁出 CSS-in-JS 的。

Primer 设计系统支撑着您如今在 GitHub 上看到的许多体验。从按钮到横幅再到面包屑导航，这些基础组件都必须在各种场景下兼顾无障碍访问性、灵活性与高性能。

早在 2023 年，某些页面上的组件数量开始出现爆发式增长。这给我们现有的 CSS-in-JS 解决方案带来了一些与性能相关的挑战：

很明显，Primer 团队需要从源头上解决该问题。我们必须找到一种替代方案，彻底避免当前方案所带来的客户端和服务器端开销。最重要的是，我们选择的任何替代方案在迁移过程中都必须确保不会对 GitHub 造成任何破坏。

Primer 团队找到了一种符合我们全部标准的解决方案：CSS Modules。这种格式使我们能够实践最喜欢的事情之一：编写并使用原生 CSS 特性，同时依然保留我们以往从 CSS-in-JS 中所期望的一定程度的就近部署与样式封装。

借助 CSS Modules，样式可以在组件对应的 JavaScript 源文件旁以独立的 CSS 文件进行编写。它还允许我们将所有类名默认视为局部作用域，从而避免全局选择器可能带来的一些命名冲突与挑战。这种格式还消除了对任何客户端或服务器端运行时的需求。取而代之的是，样式将被打包汇总进 CSS 样式表中，作为页面 HTML 的一部分进行下发。

然而，这一方案与我们当时采用的 CSS-in-JS 方案截然不同。这一变更需要对每一个 Primer 组件以及 GitHub 中使用该技术编写的每一个组件进行更新。值得庆幸的是，设计系统正是大规模交付此类变更的绝佳载体。

转向 CSS Modules 的形势已经十分明朗。Primer 团队需要对旗下每个组件进行更新，将其从 CSS-in-JS 迁移至 CSS Modules。与此同时，我们对这些组件所做的更新绝不能破坏其在 GitHub 中的任何既有使用。最后，我们用于 CSS-in-JS 的底层技术也必须对 GitHub 中目前正在使用它的所有组件保持正常运作。

在所有这些约束条件下，我们决定采取渐进式迁移策略，以便在不破坏任何现有功能的前提下安全交付组件更新。对于每个组件，我们的计划如下：

这一流程建立起了一个强大的反馈闭环，随着 Primer 持续向 GitHub 交付这些变更，问题在早期阶段就能被发现并标记。功能特性开关（feature flags）的使用让我们能够安全推进此次迁移，同时为我们提供了有关 CSS Modules 性能收益的明确信号。

截至 2024 年 12 月，Primer 中的所有组件均已通过此流程迁移至 CSS Modules。我们观察到了全方位的性能提升，特别是：

鉴于在 Primer 中开展这项工作获得了显著的性能提升，我们开始思考：如果在 GitHub 的其他部分也进行此类转换，是否也能获得类似的性能增益？同样，我们需要多久才能最终在整个公司范围内彻底废止对 CSS-in-JS 的支持？

从 Primer 中移除 CSS-in-JS 方案最棘手的部分之一在于 sx 属性（sx prop）的使用。该属性曾是为 Primer 组件添加样式和进行自定义的标准途径。各个团队可以通过传入内联对象来自定义该组件的一切样式。它代表了 CSS-in-JS 最出色但也最糟糕的方面：

因此，我们告别 CSS-in-JS 之旅的第一步，就是减少整个 GitHub 中 sx 的使用。这将使我们能够立即获得性能提升，类似于迁移 Primer 组件时看到的收益。这也为我们从产品中彻底移除 CSS-in-JS 奠定了绝佳的基础。

值得注意的是，尽管设计系统本身已正式脱离 styled-components，但 GitHub 代码库本身的很大一部分尚未脱离。由于 sx 属性多年来一直是 GitHub 事实上的样式标准，我们面临着数以千计需要迁移的 sx 属性，之后才谈得上让 GitHub 用上全新且不依赖 styled-components 的 @primer/react 版本。

那么……我们究竟是如何在提升确定性并降低风险的同时，完成这一庞大工作量的呢？答案是：切忌一蹴而就。

最初的 CSS 迁移比我们之前透露的要更为微妙：除了将组件迁移到 CSS Modules、利用特性开关在生产环境中进行测试并逐步灰度推广之外，我们还在一个名为 @primer/styled-react 的过渡库中创建了“包装器（wrapper）”组件。该软件包的全部目的就是允许在刚完成迁移的组件中继续使用 sx。这样一来，GitHub UI 代码库中使用该属性的实例可以通过从 @primer/styled-react 导入同一组件来继续使用它们；而对于未使用该属性的场景，我们则可以通过直接从 @primer/react 导入来收获性能红利。

下一阶段的迁移流程如下：

说来也巧，正当我们准备着手开展这项艰巨工程时，styled-components 宣布进入维护模式，这进一步印证了我们的方向是正确的。

这项工作于 2025 年 4 月正式启动，待迁移的 sx 属性峰值约为 7,760 个；直到 2026 年 5 月我们才彻底实现目标。起初，我们优秀的内部开发者之一 Ian Sanders 创建了一个 VS Code 插件来辅助逐个属性的迁移。内部还开发了类似的 codemod 工具，并将其用于迁移 GitHub 代码库中的整个文件。这项工作虽然需要少量人工核查和细致验证，但绝大部分已实现自动化。由 8 名工程师轮值组成的团队在 6 个月内迁移了 6,419 个属性，观察到服务端渲染（SSR）时间性能提升在不同页面中从 1% 到 22% 不等。

而在 GitHub 的另一个方向，Copilot 的能力正在呈指数级增长。AI 变得更加聪明、更加强大；在推进这项工作期间，我们相继发布了 Copilot 编码代理（Copilot coding agent）和 Copilot 代码评审（Copilot code review）。

当我们重新接手这项工作时（已是 2026 年 4 月），局面已大不相同；在由两名工程师组成的团队、坚定的决心以及大量 Copilot 编码代理的通力协作下，我们在短短三周内将待处理的 sx 属性从 895 个彻底清零。

那是一个重大时刻：历经数年筹划，我们终于完成了阻挡在我们与彻底移除 styled-components 之间的所有 sx 迁移……我们终于可以清理这些依赖项，转而投入其他更令人兴奋的工作了，对吧？大错特错！

GitHub 支持七种不同的主题，所有主题都提供了高对比度模式变体。正如你所猜想的，这一切全部是通过 styled-components 实现的。在考虑移除这些依赖之前，我们必须先对主题系统进行解耦。

不过，这并没有听起来那么严重。我们的主题变量一直是通过 @primer/css 软件包在 CSS 中定义的，而且在 2025 年末迁移 @primer/react 时，我们就已经为非 styled 的主题化方案做好了规划。我们需要移除的，其实是 styled-components 所支持的 JavaScript 用法和实用工具。我们再一次投入到了工作中。

此时你大概也清楚常规套路了：执行迁移、逐步灰度推进、为所有功能加上特性开关（feature flag）。历时两个月并经历了一些小波折之后，我们全面做好了移除依赖的准备；我们甚至连移除依赖本身也配置了特性开关。毕竟防患于未然总是好的。

截至 2026 年 6 月，GitHub 已经完全在 100% 的 CSS 模块（CSS Modules）上运行。我们设立的安全保障措施使我们能够安全地推出重大的架构变革、在生产环境中进行压力测试、捕获错误、高效调整并修复，最终让我们达成了目标，并在整个过程中实现了巨大的性能提升。

起初看似只是一次 CSS 迁移，最终证明是一场关于 GitHub 如何在大规模场景下进行样式设计、主题化以及交付 UI 的渐进式平台重构。到最后，我们不仅从主站（dotcom）中彻底移除了 sx、styled-components 和 styled-system，而且在整个过程中没有对 GitHub 造成任何破坏。提升我们产品的性能、用户体验和愉悦感，始终是我们在 GitHub 每一个人的重中之重。

Josh Black 是一名常驻得克萨斯州奥斯汀的软件工程师。他热衷于从事设计系统开发、打造无障碍体验，以及品尝墨西哥红烩炸玉米片（chilaquiles）。

Marie 是 GitHub Primer 团队驻亚特兰大的软件工程师。如果不忙于微调像素，她大概正在大西洋上空的某个航班上，把随身行李塞进头顶的行李架里。

如果你能把工作流程写下来，你就能将其自动化。以下是我为支持 GitHub 亚太区营销团队所做的工作。

我们为 GitHub 无障碍扫描器构建了一个插件，以确保你的替代文本（alt text）真正具备无障碍可用性。以下是它的运作原理。

我们是如何重构 GitHub Copilot 应用中的差异对比界面的，从而能够打开包含数百万行代码变动和数百条行内审查评论的拉取请求（Pull Request）。

为什么较短的输出反而成本更高，以及 GitHub Copilot 如何在整个编码任务中减少无用功。

精通 GitHub 所需的一切，尽在一处。

在 GitHub 上构建未来，这里是世界各地任何人构建任何东西的平台。

走近利用 GitHub 进行构建的企业和工程团队。

欢迎于 10 月 28 日至 29 日在旧金山或在线参与我们的年度旗舰开发者盛会 GitHub Universe，在这里汇聚人类、智能体（agents）以及全世界的代码。

trendStories.title: 在 p5.js 中讲授 GPU 编程：现已支持计算着色器
trendStories.originalTitle: Teaching GPU programming in p5.js: now with compute shaders
trendStories.fullContent:
Computer graphics education is in a weird place right now. The graphical capabilities of computers have expanded tremendously. At this point, it's also hard to talk about "graphical" capabilities: your Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is no longer just pushing triangles onto the screen; it's a platform for general parallel programming. That's fantastic for increasing the possibilities! But with so much potentially to learn, how do you get started?

There is a lot of background context generally required in order to do any programming for the GPU, which makes it notoriously hard to get into. Rendering a triangle in Vulkan from scratch takes thousands of lines of code. This is a problem professors teaching computer graphics are currently grappling with. The playbook that seems to be solidifying is to not teach everything at first, and provide a template to work within that hides the bits that aren't initially relevant to the learning. As students learn more, the scaffolding can incrementally be pulled away, and they can become aware of those initially hidden parts. But, importantly, those hidden bits are not necessary for making immediate initial progress. This technique is called scaffolded learning.

Currently, everyone's wandering on their own trying to figure out what scaffolding to use. Often, scaffolding abstracts away many of the underlying graphics API, but leaves in place much of the "classic" shader pipeline: students still need to learn how data flows through vertex to fragment shaders, how data is passed from the CPU to the GPU, and how to write shader code in a new language. While this is still simplified compared to starting completely from scratch, that's still a lot to jump into.

I help develop p5.js. Alongside being a tool for artists, it is often used as a computer science teaching tool, conveniently making it easy to visualize logic. That has mostly been done with its 2D mode, so introductory 3D and GPU teaching has tended to favour tools like three.js instead. Over the past few years, I've been trying to fill in the GPU gaps in p5.

After releasing an experimental WebGPU build of p5.js earlier this year, working a little on performance, and fixing a lot of bugs, I've been able to start implementing compute shaders. That last puzzle piece brings p5 much closer to the goal of being the GPU learning system I'd like it to be. So let's talk about what that looks like!

The emerging goal for p5.strands, our shader system, is to provide scaffolding such that if you have made a p5.js sketch before and are familiar with, for example, the Introduction to p5.js category of tutorials on the p5 site, you should be able to have an easy first step into GPU programming. You should always be able to be productive and make interesting things at every skill level, and each incremental piece you learn helps you achieve a specific new capability on top of what you already could do. While abstractions can be simplifying, none should be misleading; you should not need to unlearn any bad habits in order to later jump from p5 to more engineering-oriented systems. That said, p5 should not just be a learning tool: the abstractions should be convenient and intuitive enough that you'd want to use them, regardless of skill level, until your project hits a scale and scope that turns it into a larger engineering project.

We're pretty explicit about what we think you do and don't need to know to start using p5.strands:

The API has been carefully updated so that you don't need more than that to start. You do not need to know about the shader pipeline, uniforms, varying variables, or anything like that at first. You will still learn those things! But they are not required upfront like they would otherwise be; they stay out of the way until you need them.

After having used existing p5 filters such as filter(BLUR), it is not a huge jump to create your own filters. It involves creating a function, using arrays, and working with properties and methods of objects. The biggest thing to learn is the special filterColor object, which you can .set() with a color. Here's a filter that makes the canvas red! Nothing fancy yet, but you can see that colors go from 0 to 1.

filterColor also has a property texCoord saying what coordinate of the canvas texture you're on. That conveniently also goes from 0 to 1 in both axes, so you can visualize it as a color easily. The resulting gradient is illustrative of how the function gets run on each pixel with different inputs.

You can explore generative textures by passing those coordinates into noise(). Of course, you can also make your own noise function if you'd like to learn what it's doing under the hood. But it's a useful and productive construct that is already familiar from the rest of p5.

You can even create animations by using p5.js time functions like millis() like you normally would. For people who already know shaders: under the hood, this involves some uniforms, but the learner does not need to be aware of this yet. They can instead focus on the biggest conceptual leap of writing a fragment shader, which is the fact that your same code needs to run on every pixel. This inversion from the usual way you draw in p5 can be the main focus, with surprisingly few limitations, until the learner feels comfortable.

A natural point to introduce uniforms is when you want to reference a value from a slider. With uniformFloat, we can pass in a slider value and then use that to adjust the animation from before:

A next step can be to show how shaders can be used on objects, not just on the pixels of the whole canvas. Every vertex (a term familiar already from beginShape/endShape drawing) also can be modified by a shader, if you do so in the right block. In p5.strands, the way to do this is the worldInputs block, where you can modify vertex positions in world space. This can be used to move an object around:

Of course, you don't need a shader to do the above in p5 already. But it then lets you do some additional things. For example, you can apply a different offset to each vertex. You could do this with a for loop and beginShape/endShape, but it's very tedious to do, and requires you to suddenly create all the vertices yourself. Here, I can just take the previous shader but use the vertex position in the math:

When you introduce the ability to draw an object with multiple instances, updating positions in a shader becomes extra useful.

If you're already drawing an object with a function, as I did above, you can create a reusable model out of it with buildGeometry. Then, you can draw it with model(geometry, count), and pass in the number of instances of that model you want to draw. You can then position them differently in the shader based on which iteration is being drawn, accessible via instanceID().

You can already do a lot with this! If you need to move things along prescribed paths, this will work just fine, and you can draw a lot more copies than you would be able to do with a for loop before it starts to lag. Here's an example of drawing a ton of lines with slightly different colors at slightly different positions to create the effect of light dispersion.

But not every kind of motion can be driven by noise() or sin() or other predetermined functions. What if I have a bunch of specific locations I want to position points at? Or if each particle needs to move independently? See, for example, the Nature of Code chapter on autonomous agents. Lots of cool techniques in there!

WebGPU starts to get us there. The examples from here on out will require you to use a browser with WebGPU support, which Chrome and Firefox on Windows and Mac should have now in their latest versions.

We can create storage buffers with createStorage that you can read in a shader with uniformStorage. Here's a simple version of that where we hard-code a few locations for objects. Note that we await createCanvas(w, h, WEBGPU) now!

Ok, three hardcoded positions for spheres isn't that exciting. Here's what that looks like with more complicated position data that I'm extracting from an SVG:

When you have data in a storage buffer, the next logical step is to ask how to update that data to make the particles move. That's how you would implement the agents described in Nature of Code. Interactions are described via how you would incrementally update state every frame rather than having a formula for the exact position given time.

Typically that would be done with a for loop, but with WebGPU, you can now do that with a compute shader using buildComputeShader. Compute shaders are like for loops, but instead of doing one iteration after the other, they instead run all iterations at once in parallel, something that needs special hardware—your GPU—to accomplish.

For comparison, here's some code to make a bunch of balls bounce off the walls of the canvas with no compute shaders, using a regular for loop. Afterwards, we'll show what this looks like in a compute shader.

Now here's the compute shader version. Rather than using just an array, we use a storage buffer. The update function now just does one iteration of the loop, using index.x to keep track of the current iteration. Drawing all the particles is also done all at once with a shader and instanceID(). You run the update by calling compute() and passing in your shader.

Compute shaders get interesting because, roughly, you can run a loop on thousands of things in the time it would normally take to run just one iteration of a regular for loop. This means you can do stuff that would otherwise take a lot of algorithmic complexity to run quickly. Do you wanted to make all the balls bounce off of each other? The double-nested for loop approach can get slow in regular JavaScript. No problem in a WebGPU compute shader though. I'll also give them some different radii for the fun of it.

Going back to Nature of Code, here's an implementation of the boids flocking algorithm. This is just a little window with 100 agents, but I've got a fullscreen sketch version that runs nicely with ten thousand agents on my M1 Macbook Pro. Without having to think about spatial partitioning algorithms at all!

For another example, the header of this page was created using an n-body gravity simulation with points sampled from text, which you can run and inspect for yourself on OpenProcessing.

We've built out a system that slowly exposes you to vertex shaders, fragment shaders, compute shaders, uniforms, varying variables, and textures as they become useful to you.

You can also slowly expand into platform-native shader languages, too–every block in p5.strands can also be filled in via a function in GLSL or WGSL. The same animated gradient from earlier looks like this in GLSL:

If you wanted to see how a JavaScript shader would look as a native shader, you can call .inspectHooks() on it, and it will print the native implementation of your JavaScript.

So, even when you outgrow the JS shader system, you can still hook into the p5 default shaders with native shader code, so you don't have to redo the entirety of p5's positioning and material systems. Then, of course, there are the loadShader and createShader functions you can call if you truly need to start from scratch, or want to learn how to make the whole thing yourself.

I hope that at that point, you'll have all the understanding you'll need to fearlessly jump into whatever other GPU library or hardware platform you need. You'll still have some learning to do, but by that point, you won't be faced with a mountain of new things; instead, it'll be a matter of learning how the new system handles the concepts you already know.

p5.strands in WebGL is already live, and compute shaders will land in the next release of p5.js, version 2.3 (but you can test it out from the build of the compute shader branch right now.) If you start exploring GPU programming with these tools, please do join the p5.js Discord server and let us know how it goes! We are hoping to continuously refine and improve the experience, and hearing from you can help shape development. Similarly, if you're hoping to try teaching with p5, we'd also love to hear from you about how we can improve things for you and your students.

My name is Dave and I'm a programmer and artist. All content created by hand. Want to get in touch? Find or contact me elsewhere:

dave@davepagurek.com GitHub RSS Mastodon Instagram YouTube Soundcloud Sarcastic Soundcloud Newgrounds CodePen
trendStories.fullTranslation:
计算机图形学教育目前正处于一个尴尬的境地。计算机的图形处理能力已经实现了巨大的飞跃。在当前阶段，甚至很难单纯去谈论“图形”能力：你的图形处理器（GPU）已不再仅仅是把三角形推送到屏幕上；它已经成为一个通用并行计算平台。这对于拓展可能性来说固然极为出色！但有如此之多潜在的内容需要学习，你该如何入门？

要在 GPU 上进行任何编程，通常都需要大量的背景知识储备，这使得它的入门门槛高得出了名。在 Vulkan 中从零开始渲染一个三角形需要成千上万行代码。这是目前讲授计算机图形学的教授们正苦苦思索应对的问题。逐渐形成的一种通用做法是不要一开始就讲授全部内容，而是提供一个内置模板供人操作，隐藏掉那些初期与学习无关的细节。随着学生了解的内容逐渐深入，可以逐步撤去“脚手架”，让他们逐渐了解那些最初隐藏的部分。但最重要的一点在于，这些隐藏的细节对于取得即时的初步进展并非必需。这种教学技巧被称为脚手架式学习（scaffolded learning）。

目前，大家都在各自摸索该采用怎样的脚手架。脚手架通常会抽象掉许多底层的图形 API，但依然保留了大部分“经典”的着色器管线（shader pipeline）：学生仍需要学习数据如何从顶点着色器流向片元着色器、数据如何从 CPU 传递到 GPU，以及如何用一门全新的语言编写着色器代码。尽管比起完全从头开始这已经有所简化，但要想跨入这道门槛依然负担沉重。

我参与了 p5.js 的开发。它除了是艺术家们的工具外，还经常被用作计算机科学的教学工具，能非常方便地将逻辑可视化。以往这主要是在其 2D 模式下进行的，因此入门级 3D 和 GPU 教学往往更倾向于使用诸如 three.js 等工具。在过去的几年里，我一直在努力填补 p5 在 GPU 方面的空白。

在今年早些时候发布了 p5.js 的实验性 WebGPU 构建版本、在性能上做了些优化并修复了大量 Bug 之后，我终于能够着手实现计算着色器（compute shaders）了。这最后一块拼图让 p5 距离成为我所期望的 GPU 学习系统又近了一大步。那么，让我们来聊聊它究竟是什么样子的吧！

我们的着色器系统 p5.strands 逐渐确立的目标，是提供这样一种脚手架：如果你以前编写过 p5.js 的作品（sketch），并且熟悉诸如 p5 官网上的“p5.js 入门”系列教程，那么你就应该能轻松迈出 GPU 编程的第一步。无论处于何种技能水平，你都应该始终能够有所产出并做出有趣的东西，而且你所学到的每一块递进知识，都能帮助你在原有能力的基础上解锁一项具体的新功能。虽然抽象可以起到简化的作用，但绝不能产生误导；你绝不需要为了日后从 p5 转向更面向工程的系统而强行摒弃任何坏习惯。话说回来，p5 绝不应该仅仅是一个学习工具：其抽象层应当足够便捷和直观，以至于无论你的技能水平如何，你都会愿意使用它们，直到你的项目规模和体量大到变成了一个更庞大的工程项目为止。

关于要开始使用 p5.strands 我们认为你需要知道什么和不需要知道什么，我们的态度是非常明确的：

该 API 经过了细致的更新，因此你无需掌握更多内容即可开始。你一开始完全不需要了解着色器管线、uniform 变量、varying 变量或类似的概念。你最终依然会学到这些东西！但它们不再像以前那样被强制要求提前掌握；在真正需要它们之前，它们都不会来干扰你。

在熟悉了 filter(BLUR) 等现有 p5 滤镜后，创建属于自己的滤镜就绝非什么难事了。它涉及创建一个函数、使用数组，以及操作对象的属性和方法。最需要学习的重点是特殊的 filterColor 对象，你可以通过 .set() 为其设置颜色。下面是一个将画布变红的滤镜！虽然还不算复杂，但你可以看到颜色取值范围在 0 到 1 之间。

filterColor 还有一个名为 texCoord 的属性，用来表示你当前处于画布纹理的哪个坐标上。极为方便的是，它在两个轴向上的取值也都是 0 到 1，因此你可以轻松地将其直观展示为一种颜色。所生成的渐变效果生动说明了该函数是如何以不同的输入在每个像素上运行的。

你可以通过将这些坐标传入 noise() 来探索生成式纹理。当然，如果你想了解其底层运作原理，也可以自己编写噪声函数。但这是一个非常实用且高效的结构，而且在 p5 的其他部分中大家已经对其十分熟悉了。

你甚至可以像平时一样，使用 millis() 等 p5.js 时间函数来创建动画。对于已经了解着色器的人来说：在底层，这涉及一些 uniform 变量，但初学者目前还不需要意识到这一点。相反，他们可以集中精力克服编写片元着色器时最大的概念飞跃——即你的同一段代码需要在每个像素上运行这一事实。在初学者感到适应之前，这种对 p5 常规绘制方式的倒置可以作为主要关注点，且受到的限制出奇地少。

引入 uniform 变量的一个自然契机，是当你想要引用滑块（slider）的值时。通过 uniformFloat，我们可以传入一个滑块值，然后用它来调整前面的动画：

下一步可以展示如何将着色器应用到物体上，而不仅仅是应用在整个画布的像素上。每一个顶点（在 beginShape/endShape 绘制中已经熟知的概念）也都可以被着色器修改，前提是你在正确的代码块中进行操作。在 p5.strands 中，实现这一功能的方式是 worldInputs 块，在其中你可以在世界空间中修改顶点位置。这可以用来移动一个物体：

当然，在 p5 中要实现上述效果本来就不需要着色器。但接着它能让你完成一些额外的事情。例如，你可以给每个顶点应用不同的偏移量。虽然你可以使用 for 循环配合 beginShape/endShape 来完成这项操作，但做起来非常繁琐，并且迫使你突然要自己去创建所有的顶点。而在此时，我只需要沿用前面的着色器，但在数学计算中使用顶点位置即可：

当你引入绘制具有多个实例（instances）的对象的能力时，在着色器中更新位置就变得格外有用了。

如果你已经像我上面那样用函数绘制了一个对象，就可以使用 buildGeometry 将其制作成可复用的模型。然后，你可以通过 model(geometry, count) 绘制它，并传入你希望绘制该模型的实例数量。接着，你可以在着色器中根据当前绘制的是哪一个迭代（通过 instanceID() 访问）来将它们放置在不同的位置。

仅仅依靠这个，你其实就已经能做很多事情了！如果你需要让物体沿着指定路径运动，这种方式完全适用；而且在出现卡顿之前，你能绘制的副本数量要远远多于使用 for 循环所能达到的量。这里有一个示例：在略有差异的位置绘制大量颜色微调的线条，以此营造出光的色散效果。

但并非所有类型的运动都能由 noise()、sin() 或其他预定函数来驱动。如果我想把点放置在一堆特定位置上呢？或者如果每个粒子都需要独立运动呢？例如，可以参考《代码本色》（Nature of Code）中关于自主智能体（autonomous agents）的章节，里面有很多非常酷的技术！

WebGPU 开始帮我们实现这一点。接下来的示例需要你使用支持 WebGPU 的浏览器，目前 Windows 和 Mac 平台最新版本的 Chrome 和 Firefox 应该都已支持。

我们可以使用 createStorage 创建存储缓冲区（storage buffers），并在着色器中通过 uniformStorage 来读取它。这里展示了一个简单版本，其中硬编码了几个物体的位置。请注意，我们现在需要使用 await createCanvas(w, h, WEBGPU) 了！

好吧，三个硬编码的球体位置确实不算特别令人兴奋。下面展示的是使用我从 SVG 中提取的更复杂位置数据时的效果：

当你在存储缓冲区中有了数据之后，下一个顺理成章的问题就是如何更新这些数据以让粒子运动。这就是实现《代码本色》中所描述的智能体的方式。交互是通过每一帧如何逐步更新状态来描述的，而不是依赖于在给定时间下计算确切位置的现成公式。

通常这会通过 for 循环来完成，但有了 WebGPU，你现在可以使用 buildComputeShader 配合计算着色器（compute shader）来实现。计算着色器类似于 for 循环，但它并不是按顺序一次执行一个迭代，而是同时并行运行所有迭代——这需要特定的硬件（即你的 GPU）来完成。

为了进行对比，这里有一段不使用计算着色器、仅使用普通 for 循环让一堆球在画布边缘反弹的代码。稍后，我们将展示在计算着色器中这是如何实现的。

现在来看计算着色器的版本。我们使用的是存储缓冲区，而不再仅仅是一个普通数组。更新函数现在只执行循环中的单次迭代，并使用 index.x 来跟踪当前迭代。绘制所有粒子也是通过着色器配合 instanceID() 一次性完成的。你只需调用 compute() 并传入你的着色器即可运行更新。

计算着色器之所以强大有趣，是因为大致来说，在普通 for 循环通常只能运行单次迭代的时间里，它可以在成千上万个对象上并发运行循环。这意味着你可以执行一些通常需要极高算法复杂度才能快速运行的操作。想让所有的球互相碰撞反弹吗？在常规 JavaScript 中，双重嵌套 for 循环的方式可能会变得很慢。但在 WebGPU 计算着色器中完全没问题。为了好玩，我还为它们设置了不同的大小半径。

再次回到《代码本色》，这里是 Boids 鸟群聚集算法的一个实现。这只是一个仅有 100 个智能体的小窗口，但我有一个全屏草图版本，在我的 M1 MacBook Pro 上运行一万个智能体时依然流畅。完全无需考虑空间分割算法！

再举一个例子，本页面的顶部横幅是使用基于文本采样的点进行的 N 体引力模拟制作的，你可以在 OpenProcessing 上亲自运行并查看代码。

我们构建了一个系统，它会随着各项功能对你产生实用价值，逐步向你介绍顶点着色器（vertex shaders）、片元着色器（fragment shaders）、计算着色器（compute shaders）、uniform 变量、varying 变量以及纹理。

你也可以逐步过渡到平台原生的着色语言——p5.strands 中的每个代码块都可以用 GLSL 或 WGSL 函数来编写。前面提到的同一个动态渐变效果在 GLSL 中是这样的：

如果你想看看 JavaScript 着色器在原生着色器中是什么样子，可以在其上调用 .inspectHooks()，它就会打印出 JavaScript 代码的原生实现。

因此，即使你不再满足于 JS 着色器系统，你仍然可以用原生着色器代码接入 p5 的默认着色器，这样就不必重写 p5 的整个定位和材质系统。当然，如果你确实需要从头开始构建，或者想学习如何完全自主编写，还可以调用 loadShader 和 createShader 函数。

我希望到了那个阶段，你能够掌握足够的知识，毫不畏惧地跨入所需的任何其他 GPU 库或硬件平台。你仍然会有一些新东西需要学习，但届时摆在你面前的将不再是堆积如山的新概念；相反，这只是一个了解新系统如何处理你早已掌握的那些概念的过程。

WebGL 中的 p5.strands 已经上线，而计算着色器将在 p5.js 的下一个版本（2.3 版本）中正式推出（但你现在就可以通过计算着色器分支的构建版本来进行测试）。如果你开始使用这些工具探索 GPU 编程，请务必加入 p5.js 的 Discord 服务器，并告诉我们你的使用体验！我们希望能不断完善和优化体验，倾听你的反馈有助于推动开发。同样，如果你打算尝试用 p5 进行教学，我们也十分期待听到你的意见，了解我们如何为你和你的学生改进工具。
